Our question

Current resource savings and future investment operate on different timescales. Prices can adjust when a technology changes, while learning and research accumulate over time. Our mathematical task is to find a path where current decisions, those accumulated changes, and expected future returns remain consistent.

We organize that task around current allocation, inherited states, and future valuation. Expertise EEE and the frontier AAA carry earlier decisions into the present. Qualification value Δ\DeltaΔ brings later opportunities into today’s investment. Their connection turns a sequence of market allocations into one dynamic equilibrium (fig. 9).

This organization also determines how we compare changes. We can hold a frontier fixed to isolate a market response, compare stationary occupations to study lasting training adjustments, or follow a full transition after an announcement. Each comparison answers a different question about the same economy.

Choices and states

Current markets allocate what the economy already has. Customers select services, workers choose instruction, and research procurement chooses among feasible methods. One wage connects customer demand to research costs wherever both activities use qualified labor. This shared price makes their allocations depend on each other.

Inherited states record changes that take time. Training and experience add qualifications, obsolescence removes them, and completed research advances the frontier. Keeping these accumulated quantities separate from current choices lets us distinguish reallocating existing expertise from creating more of it.

Forward and backward

We specify initial conditions for EEE and AAA, and a terminal payoff for Δ\DeltaΔ. These conditions describe different economic commitments. Initial states say what earlier generations have left available. Terminal value says what a qualification will be worth beyond the interval we study. Together they connect an inherited economy to the future its workers anticipate.

Equilibrium requires those expectations to agree with the earnings the path produces. Study changes future labor supply, which changes the wages used to value study today. We solve this mutual dependence across the whole path. Announced changes can consequently affect investment before they alter current production.

Key results

Our finite-horizon result gives conditions for a unique equilibrium within a specified feasible region over a sufficiently short horizon. For longer horizons, a local selection condition identifies a nearby solution. These results explain how inherited states and future payoffs select the paths used in our comparisons.

Future wage differences enter current qualification value with positive weights when terminal values agree. This gives a direct interpretation of anticipation. Earnings expected further along a career already matter for current training, and the full path determines their combined effect.

Growth depends on the productivity of a complete research method. Within a method, the slower-improving required stage sets its eventual exponent. Across available methods, procurement selects the cheaper route. Under the stated input-price and continuation conditions, comparison with research difficulty separates power growth, exponential order, and a finite production endpoint.

Research timing changes that classification. Gradual absorption can preserve a finite production endpoint at high productivity, while a positive minimum research duration keeps the frontier finite at every finite date. Superexponential growth can still occur in the latter case. This result distinguishes how fast capability grows from whether it becomes unbounded in finite time.

Equation guide

We start with the equilibrium chapter, which defines customer costs, private study, wages, and research production. Dynamics connects inherited states to future earnings and explains the response relationships in the economy diagram. RSI and growth follows complete-method productivity and research timing, and Derivations supplies the intermediate steps. Reading the story introduction gives the economic interpretation of the same sequence.
